turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Dinosaurs ruled the Earth for more than one hundred fifty million years. What happened to them?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Most scientists believe a giant asteroid hit the Earth about sixty-six million years ago. It was probably around ten kilometers wide.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: An important clue came in nineteen eighty. Scientists found a thin layer of rock all around the world, from exactly that time. It contained a lot of a rare metal called iridium. Iridium is uncommon on the Earth's surface but more common in asteroids.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: So the asteroid's dust spread across the planet.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Exactly. Later, scientists found a huge buried crater in Mexico, about one hundred eighty kilometers wide. It's the right size and the right age.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: But how could one impact kill so many animals?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: The impact threw huge amounts of dust and gas into the atmosphere. It blocked sunlight for a long time. Plants struggled to grow, temperatures dropped, and food chains collapsed. About three-quarters of all species disappeared.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Was the asteroid the only cause?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Some scientists think huge volcanic eruptions in India also played a role, by changing the climate. The debate continues, but the asteroid is the main suspect.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Not exactly. Birds are actually living dinosaurs. So the next time you see a pigeon, you're looking at a distant relative of T. rex.
